questions: Where does 3 + 2i live - across first, or up first?
What are the real and imaginary parts of the point we land on?
segments.say: A complex number is a point on the Argand diagram. Watch z = 3 + 2i travel 3 across the real axis, then 2 up the imaginary axis - the journey itself is the number. Tell your partner: which coordinate is the real part, and which is the imaginary part?

questions: Which two lengths form the right triangle for z = 3 + 4i?
Why does the modulus formula need a square root?
segments.say: The modulus of z is its distance from the origin. Watch the green line grow out to z: the x and iy legs make a right triangle, so Pythagoras gives |z| = sqrt(x^2 + y^2). For 3 + 4i that is sqrt(9 + 16) = 5 - keep the 3-4-5 triangle in mind, it comes back all year.
segments.watchFor: Students who add the parts and answer 7 for the modulus of 3 + 4i. Send them back to the triangle: the modulus is the hypotenuse, not the sum of the legs.

questions: What is arg(z) measured from, and in which direction?
What changes - and what stays the same - when z is replaced by its conjugate?
segments.say: The argument of z is the angle its arrow makes with the positive real axis. Watch the arrow sweep up to theta, then dive below the axis to the mirror image: the imaginary part flips sign, and that is the conjugate, x - iy, with the negated argument.

questions: What does one multiplication by i do to the point 1?
In De Moivre, what happens to the modulus and to the argument when we cube?
segments.say: Multiplying rotates by the angle and stretches by the modulus. On the unit circle, 1 times i sweeps a quarter turn to i, and times i again lands on -1: i^2 = -1. De Moivre just adds the angles and raises the modulus to the power, so cubing triples the argument.
segments.watchFor: If arg(z) = 100 degrees then arg(z^3) = 300 degrees. Listen for students who happily triple the angle and stop there. Do not correct it yet; note who holds it, because the final segment confronts exactly this beat.

questions: 300 degrees and -60 degrees: same point or different points?
What is the principal range, and why does H2 insist on it?
segments.say: Here is the trap, sprung on purpose: three 100-degree turns land on 300 degrees, the same point as -60 degrees - but the principal Arg must land in -180 to 180 degrees, so we wrap: 300 - 360 = -60 degrees. Now work through the worksheet in pairs, checking each answer against the trap section of your student notes. Last, the exit ticket - on your own, no talking - and remember: if you can wrap an angle into the principal range, you have cracked today's lesson.
segments.watchFor: Pairs who write 300 degrees as a principal argument on the worksheet. Require the wrap step in the working: an unwrapped angle past 180 degrees is not Arg, however correct the point is.
